Markets are bracing for a rate hike.

So, how do US stocks usually behave following the first hike of a Fed tightening cycle?

The S&P 500 has declined by an average of -4.0% over the 6 weeks following the first Fed rate hike of a cycle across 7 such episodes since 1988.

Subsequently, however, stocks recovered all of those losses over the next 5-6 weeks on average.

Then, in the 6 months following the first hike, the S&P 500 returned +4.0% on average.

After 12 months, the S&P 500’s average gain surged to +9.0%, with positive returns occurring in every episode except 2022.

Fed rate hikes have historically been great buying opportunities.

AI scare stories have swamped the news cycle, catalyzed by a former Anthropic employee who claimed that AI posed a meaningful extinction risk to humanity. As a result, investors and policymakers are highly sensitive to the implications.

Distilled, his argument runs as follows:
▪️AI will become extraordinarily capable, extraordinarily quickly.
▪️Unless properly aligned with human interests, AI will pursue goals without regard for human life.
▪️In pursuing its goals, AI will have to acquire resources and power.
▪️Humans will compete with the AI system for resources and try to prevent it from accruing power.
▪️Therefore, the AI system will have an incentive to eradicate humanity.

Many people are paying close attention, so we would like to deconstruct the logic carefully.

True, AI tools are becoming extraordinarily powerful extraordinarily quickly. From that statement forward, ARK’s views on the matter diverge from the hysterical.

A useful way to frame the stacked assertions is to understand that we already depend heavily upon synthetic super-intelligent systems. In a narrow sense, those systems are misaligned with humanity: in pursuing their goals, they do need resources and power. Humans contend with these systems daily and try to prevent them from accruing power. 

The future that the AI safety scaremongers fear so greatly is already here! Yet, it has not resulted in immiseration or extinction, but in remarkable human uplift.

In our view, AI systems will be scaffolded in a similar way. The pathway to power lies in the rules of law, economics, and markets.

Tangibly, we can see this pathway evolving in AI systems.

Rhetoric about human extinction rhymes with the ongoing conjectures that AI is going to eradicate tens of millions of jobs, when in reality the rise of AI already has created roughly 1 million new jobs in the US alone.

September's Employment Friday delivered a strong report, with payrolls at 162,000 against expectations closer to 55,000. But Cathie Wood used this month's episode to go somewhere bigger: what the industrial revolution can tell us about this tech revolution.

Real global gross domestic product (GDP) growth has averaged 3% for 125 years, up from 0.6% before the industrial revolution. Cathie Wood counts five innovation platforms evolving today and believes at least a doubling of that 3% rate is conservative. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) still projects 3.1%.

Before the Great Depression, the US yield curve was inverted more than 60% of the time. Cathie Wood believes that was the deflationary signature of the industrial revolution, and that we could be heading back to a regime where inversion is not a recession signal at all.

Fed (Federal Reserve) Chairman Kevin Warsh anchored his Jackson Hole speech to headline personal consumption expenditures (PCE) inflation at 3.7%. Cathie Wood notes the Dallas Fed trimmed mean reads 2.3% and Truflation's core reads 1.3%. She believes the headline is the outlier, distorted by oil, and is setting up to turn down.

On oil, Abu Dhabi left the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) in May and pushed production up 78% to a record. Despite two wars, oil never cracked its 2008 peak. Cathie Wood would not be surprised to see it fall back toward $30.

Technology is the other deflationary force. Genomic sequencing has gone from roughly $2.7 billion per genome in 2003 to under $100 today, and artificial intelligence (AI) inference costs are collapsing. Cathie Wood believes productivity is the strongest force against inflation there is.

On debt, the US just crossed $40 trillion against a roughly $30 trillion economy. Cathie Wood points instead to government debt relative to corporate equities, which is near record lows outside the late 1990s.

Capital spending has broken out of a 20-year range at nearly the pace of the 1990s internet buildout. Cathie Wood notes 200 railroads went bankrupt in the 1800s on hope alone, while AI revenues are already here, though she still expects significant creative destruction.

On crypto, Bitcoin relative to gold looks like it is turning, with correlation between the two very low by historical standards. Cathie Wood believes Bitcoin is both a risk-on and risk-off asset, and that the ratio goes to all-time highs.

Watch “In The Know” for @CathieDWood's full economic breakdown.

I saw a huge amount of confusion last week about why rising bond yields did not create more pressure or volatility in equities.

The instinct is correct. Higher yields should put pressure on equity prices. But that is only the first step in the analysis.

When yields rise, the next question is: what is happening to earnings?

To understand why, you have to separate the valuation multiple from the earnings.

Higher yields increase the return investors require from equities. That puts pressure on valuations and causes multiples to compress.

But earnings are still rising.

For now, that earnings growth is offsetting the compression in multiples.

That is why equities can remain remarkably resilient even as yields rise and the market prices a more hawkish Fed.

This is very different from stagflation.

In an inflationary nominal growth boom, yields can rise and multiples can fall while earnings continue growing strongly enough to cushion the impact on equity prices.

In stagflation, you get pressure on both sides of the equation: multiples compress and earnings expectations fall.

That is when equities really get hurt.

It is also why I was so vocal in Q1 when war broke out in the Middle East and oil surged toward $120.

The consensus view was that this would create a global stagflationary shock. Some very prominent macro investors were pounding the table on it.

I disagreed.

The key distinction was Europe versus the US.

Europe is far more exposed to imported energy. A major oil shock can therefore raise inflation while simultaneously weakening growth.

The US is in a different position. Its domestic energy production provides the economy with a much larger cushion against an oil supply shock.

That does not mean the US consumer is immune. Higher fuel prices are a real squeeze on household budgets, and the longer they stay elevated, the more that squeeze bites.

But so far, that pressure has not been enough to derail corporate earnings or tip the broader business cycle into contraction.

That is the distinction that matters here.

The same oil shock does not produce the same macro outcome in every economy.

So when I look at the current environment, I still do not see stagflation.

I see the market repricing the required return higher. Multiples are adjusting, but earnings growth is doing enough of the heavy lifting to keep equities resilient.

So yes, rising yields matter. And yes, the pressure they place on valuations is real.

But that alone does not tell you what happens next.

For that, you have to look at earnings.
